Problem 1: Algorithms
Problem Statement
Let G be an edge-weighted graph. Prove that G possesses a unique minimum spanning tree
if and only if both of the following properties are satisfied: (1) For every partition of the
vertex set of G into two subsets, the edge of minimum weight connecting the two subsets is
unique. (2) For every cycle contained in G, the edge with the maximum weight is unique.
1.1
Solution
Important correction and complete solution
Throughout, let G = (V, E, w) be a finite, connected, undirected edge–weighted graph
(weights may repeat). A minimum spanning tree (MST) is a spanning tree of minimum total
weight.
The problem as stated claims: G possesses a unique MST if and only if both of the
following hold: (1) For every cut (S, V \ S), the minimum–weight edge crossing the cut is
unique. (2) For every cycle in G, the maximum–weight edge on the cycle is unique.
This “if and only if” is not correct as written: property (1) is not necessary. A standard
counterexample is the triangle with edge–weights {1, 1, 2}. Its unique MST consists of the
two edges of weight 1, yet for the cut {b} | {a, c} the two crossing edges of weight 1 tie for
the minimum, so (1) fails.
What is true is: - Property (2) is necessary and sufficient for uniqueness of the MST. -
Property (1) is sufficient (but not necessary) for uniqueness of the MST.
We now give rigorous proofs of these correct statements.
The following basic facts (cut and cycle properties) will be used repeatedly.
Cut property (strict form). If an edge e is strictly lighter than every other edge crossing
some cut, then e belongs to every MST.
Cycle property (strict form). If an edge e is strictly heavier than every other edge on
some cycle, then e belongs to no MST.
Both follow from standard exchange arguments.
Theorem A (Cycle–maximum uniqueness ⇔uniqueness of the MST). The following are
equivalent: (i) G has a unique MST. (ii) For every cycle C ⊆G, the maximum–weight edge
in C is unique.
1

Generated: 2025-12-19
Solution
Proof. (i) ⇒(ii): Suppose G has a unique MST T, and assume for contradiction that
there is a cycle C that has at least two distinct edges e ̸= f achieving the maximum weight
on C, say w(e) = w(f) = W and w(x) ≤W for all x ∈C.
Let h ∈C \ T be the unique edge of C not contained in T (every cycle omits exactly one
edge of any tree). Then h ∈C, so there is some g ∈{e, f} with g ̸= h and hence g ∈T.
Consider T ′ = T −g + h. Since h together with T creates exactly the cycle C, removing g
yields a spanning tree. Moreover,
w(T ′) = w(T) −w(g) + w(h) ≤w(T) −W + W = w(T),
with equality because w(h) ≤W = w(g). Hence T ′ is also an MST. Since g ̸= h, we have
T ′ ̸= T, contradicting uniqueness. Thus (ii) must hold.
(ii) ⇒(i): Assume (ii) and suppose, for contradiction, that there are two distinct MSTs
T ̸= T ′. Let e ∈T \ T ′. Add e to T ′; this creates a unique cycle C ⊆T ′ ∪{e}. Let x ∈C
be the unique maximum–weight edge on C, guaranteed by (ii).
If x ̸= e, then w(x) > w(e). Removing x and adding e to T ′ produces a spanning tree
T ′′ := T ′ −x + e
with strictly smaller total weight: w(T ′′) = w(T ′) −w(x) + w(e) < w(T ′), contradicting
minimality of T ′. Hence x = e. But e /∈T ′ and x ∈C ⊆T ′ ∪{e}; the only way x = e is
if e itself is the unique maximum on C. In particular, e is strictly heavier than every edge
of C \ {e}; by the cycle property (strict form), e belongs to no MST, contradicting e ∈T.
Therefore T = T ′, and the MST is unique.
Proposition B (Cut–minimum uniqueness ⇒uniqueness of the MST). If for every cut
(S, V \ S) the minimum–weight edge crossing the cut is unique, then G has a unique MST.
Proof.
Suppose, towards a contradiction, that there are two distinct MSTs T ̸= T ′.
Choose e ∈T \ T ′. Then T −e has exactly two components; let S ⊆V be the vertex–set
of one component. The edge e crosses the cut δ(S), while T ′ must contain at least one edge
f ∈T ′ ∩δ(S) to connect the two components of T −e.
By assumption, the minimum–weight edge of δ(S) is unique; since e ∈δ(S), this implies
w(e) < w(f) (because f ̸= e). Then the exchange
T ′′ := T ′ −f + e
is a spanning tree with
w(T ′′) = w(T ′) −w(f) + w(e) < w(T ′),
contradicting the minimality of T ′. Hence no two distinct MSTs exist.
Remark (Property (1) is not necessary). Consider the triangle with vertices {a, b, c} and
edge–weights w(ab) = w(bc) = 1, w(ac) = 2. The unique MST is {ab, bc} with total weight
2. However, for the cut {b} | {a, c}, the minimum–weight crossing edges {ab, bc} tie at weight
1, so property (1) fails.
Summary. - Property (2) (unique maximum on every cycle) is equivalent to uniqueness
of the MST. - Property (1) (unique minimum on every cut) is sufficient, but not necessary,
for uniqueness. - Therefore the “if and only if both (1) and (2) hold” statement is false as
written; the correct and sharp characterization is property (2).
2

fields.witness:
star+triangle; unique MST, non-unique cycle max

Graph with vertices {r,a,b,c}. Edges ra, rb, rc have weight 1; edges ab, bc, ca have weight 2. The unique MST is the star {ra,rb,rc} of total weight 3; any spanning tree using a triangle edge has weight at least 4. But the cycle a-b-c-a has three maximum-weight edges, all weight 2, so the maximum edge on that cycle is not unique.
